title: Why drummers dropped traps; Sonny Greer and Buddy Rich
summary: Crawford says Sonny Greer upset the old effects set-up and calls Buddy Rich the greatest snare drummer ever.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well, why do you think drummers stopped using, like, the temple blocks and the triangles and -- like, I've known photographs of drummers in the late 20s and early '30s, they have temple blocks, they got triangles, gong over here, they got --
Did they have all those things because of them playing, like, in shows? I mean, like, in music houses where they'd have to have effects for movies?

Yeah, yeah. And then Sonny Greer, you know, came along and upset the whole thing by having a whole complete set of drums around him, in other words, around him, such as drum outfit, temple blocks, ratchets. I don't know whether he had ratchets, maybe he didn't, but he had wood blocks, chimes, gongs, cymbals, an array of cymbals. Boy, but that Buddy Rich, nobody could touch that man, including Chick Webb.
That man is absolutely, without a doubt, bar none, to me, the greatest snare drum player that I ever saw.
Including symphony players? Does he play --

Yeah, including any of them. Symphony players, concert players, don't mention them. Throw them out of your mind. Buddy Rich, without a doubt, is the greatest snare drum player, to me, that ever lived. And he taught himself. Every time a man get those single strokes down, it's easy to do Mama-Daddy. That's double strokes. But single strokes, to me, is the foundation of all good drummers. All good drummers.
So, I can call the names and all, but thinking of them offhand is pretty hard for me. O'Neill Old Needie Spencer was another good one.
